questions.stem: About spermatogenesis in general:
options: It begins at puberty and continues without interruption until advanced age
It takes place in the epididymis
It produces spermatozoa containing 23 chromosomes
Gonocytes (primordial germ cells) first appear at puberty
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis starts at puberty, is continuous, and takes place in the seminiferous tubules of the testis, producing haploid (23-chromosome) spermatozoa. Gonocytes appear during the first weeks of embryonic development, not at puberty.

questions.stem: About the structure of the testis:
options: It is surrounded by the tunica albuginea, a poorly extensible fibrous capsule
The mediastinum testis (corpus of Highmore) is a thickening of the albuginea at the lower pole
It contains 200 to 300 lobules, each holding 1 to 4 seminiferous tubules
The seminiferous tubules of a lobule converge into a straight tubule that communicates with the rete testis
questions.explanation: The albuginea thickens at the UPPER pole to form the mediastinum testis, which contains the rete testis. Each of the 200–300 lobules holds 1–4 seminiferous tubules that drain through a 1 mm straight tubule into the rete testis.

questions.stem: A spermatozoon formed in a seminiferous tubule reaches the epididymal duct. Which route did it follow?
options: Seminiferous tubule → straight tubule → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymal duct
Seminiferous tubule → rete testis → straight tubule → efferent ductules → epididymal duct
Seminiferous tubule → straight tubule → rete testis → epididymal duct → efferent ductules
Seminiferous tubule → straight tubule → efferent ductules → rete testis → epididymal duct
questions.explanation: Tubules converge into straight tubules, which open into the rete testis (in the mediastinum); efferent ductules in the head of the epididymis then continue into the epididymal duct.

questions.stem: About the cells of the seminiferous tubule and of the interstitium:
options: Leydig cells lie in the wall of the seminiferous tubules, between the germ cells
Sertoli cells span the entire thickness of the epithelium and are linked to one another by tight junctions
From the periphery to the lumen one finds spermatogonia, primary spermatocytes, secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, then spermatozoa
Leydig cells form cords or isolated clusters around capillaries in the loose connective tissue and secrete testosterone
questions.explanation: Leydig cells are interstitial: they sit in the connective tissue BETWEEN the tubules, not in the tubule wall. The tubule wall holds only Sertoli cells and germ cells, layered from the basement membrane toward the lumen in the order of spermatogenesis.

questions.stem: About the Sertoli cell:
options: It carries membrane receptors for LH
It produces ABP (Androgen-Binding Protein)
It is a large, roughly pyramidal cell with multiple cytoplasmic processes
Germ cells divide inside its cytoplasm
questions.explanation: FSH (not LH) binds membrane receptors on Sertoli cells and stimulates ABP formation; LH acts on Leydig cells. Germ cells lie between Sertoli cells, connected to them by junctions, not inside them.

questions.stem: About the multiplication phase of spermatogenesis:
options: It concerns the spermatogonia, diploid stem cells lying against the basement membrane
Its successive mitoses maintain the spermatogonial pool
One spermatogonium gives rise to 4 primary spermatocytes
The primary spermatocytes it produces are haploid
questions.explanation: The last mitosis of the spermatogonia produces primary spermatocytes, which are still diploid (2n); haploidy is only reached after the first meiotic division.

questions.stem: About the maturation phase of spermatogenesis:
options: It is preceded by a growth phase
The primary spermatocyte undergoes the equational division
Each secondary spermatocyte gives 2 spermatids with n chromosomes
One primary spermatocyte gives 8 spermatids
questions.explanation: The primary spermatocyte (2n) undergoes the REDUCTIONAL division (meiosis I) into 2 spermatocytes II (n); each undergoes the equational division into 2 spermatids, so one spermatocyte I gives 4 spermatids.

questions.stem: Ten spermatogonia each complete one round of the sequence described in the lesson (last mitosis → meiosis). How many spermatids are obtained?
questions.explanation: One spermatogonium gives 4 primary spermatocytes, and each primary spermatocyte gives 4 spermatids, so 16 spermatids per spermatogonium, i.e. 160 for 10. 40 forgets meiosis (counts only spermatocytes I).
questions.mental: Chain the two ×4 factors: 4 × 4 = 16 spermatids per spermatogonium, then × 10 = 160. If you got 40 you stopped at the spermatocytes I; 320 doubles a step that doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Which of the following transitions involve a cell division?
options: Spermatogonium → primary spermatocyte
Primary spermatocyte → secondary spermatocytes
Spermatid → spermatozoon
Spermatozoon in the testis → motile spermatozoon in the epididymis
questions.explanation: Primary spermatocytes come from the last spermatogonial mitosis, and spermatocytes II from the first meiotic division. Spermiogenesis (spermatid → spermatozoon) involves no division, and epididymal maturation is purely functional.

questions.stem: The phases of spermatogenesis in the correct chronological order are:
options: Multiplication – growth – maturation – differentiation
Multiplication – maturation – growth – differentiation
Growth – multiplication – differentiation – maturation
Multiplication – differentiation – growth – maturation
questions.explanation: Spermatogonia multiply by mitosis, the spermatocyte I grows, meiosis forms the maturation phase, and spermiogenesis (differentiation) turns spermatids into spermatozoa.

questions.stem: About spermiogenesis:
options: It involves no cell division
The acrosome forms from the condensation of Golgi vesicles
The flagellum forms from microtubules arising from the proximal centriole
It includes a reduction of the spermatid's cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Spermiogenesis is pure differentiation: cytoplasmic reduction, an acrosome from Golgi vesicles, and a flagellum from microtubules arising from the DISTAL centriole.

questions.stem: Concerning the diagram (figure), which statement(s) is (are) correct?
options: Cell 1 renews itself, maintaining the stem-cell pool
The division from 2 to 3 is the reductional division
The transition from 1 to 2 is the first meiotic division
The transformation of 4 into 5 takes place in the epididymis
questions.explanation: 1 = spermatogonium (2n), whose mitoses both renew the pool and give primary spermatocytes (2, still 2n); 2 → 3 is meiosis I (reductional, 2n → n). 4 → 5 is spermiogenesis, which happens in the seminiferous tubule of the testis.

questions.stem: Concerning the diagram (figure), which statement(s) is (are) correct?
options: It shows the transformation of a spermatid into a spermatozoon, without division
Structure 1 derives from Golgi vesicles
Element 2 is excess cytoplasm that is eliminated
Segment 3 contains the mitochondria that supply energy for flagellar movement
questions.explanation: This is spermiogenesis: 1 is the acrosome cap (condensed Golgi vesicles), 2 the excess cytoplasm removed by cytoplasmic reduction, 3 the middle piece with its helical mitochondrial sheath.

questions.stem: Concerning the regulation diagram (figure), which statement(s) is (are) correct?
options: Cell 1 binds FSH through membrane receptors and produces ABP
Cell 2 lies in the wall of the seminiferous tubule
Product 3 is inhibin, which exerts negative feedback on FSH only
Product 4 mostly passes free into the blood
questions.explanation: 1 = Sertoli cell, 2 = Leydig cell (interstitial, outside the tubule), 3 = inhibin, 4 = testosterone. Most testosterone enters the cytoplasm and binds ABP; only the free fraction passes into the blood.

questions.stem: About the functional maturation of spermatozoa in the epididymis:
options: Spermatozoa leaving the testis are barely motile
They acquire their motility under the action of androgens secreted by the Leydig cells
They acquire their ability to fuse with the oocyte membrane
The molecules that recognize the zona pellucida are set up
questions.explanation: In the epididymis spermatozoa gain motility and zona-pellucida binding, but are DECAPACITATED by the seminal fluid: their fertilizing (fusion) ability is suppressed.

questions.stem: About decapacitation and capacitation:
options: Decapacitation occurs in the epididymis through the action of the seminal fluid
A decapacitated spermatozoon temporarily loses its ability to fuse with other membranes
To become fertilizing, the ejaculated spermatozoon must undergo capacitation in the female genital tract
The ejaculated spermatozoon is immediately able to fertilize
questions.explanation: The ejaculated spermatozoon is still decapacitated and cannot fertilize; capacitation happens later, in the female genital tract.

questions.stem: About the head of the spermatozoon:
options: The acrosome covers the posterior two-thirds of the nucleus
The nucleus occupies most of the head
The acrosome contains hyaluronidases, acrosin and the Corona Penetrating Enzyme
Its plasma membrane has particular morphological features
questions.explanation: The acrosome is a flattened vesicle over the ANTERIOR two-thirds of the nucleus, full of hydrolytic enzymes used to cross the oocyte envelopes; the plasma membrane is conventional.

questions.stem: About the neck, middle piece and flagellum of the spermatozoon:
options: The mitochondria are arranged in a helix around the flagellum in the middle piece
The mitochondria that power the flagellum are located in the end piece
The middle piece contains the centriole that gives rise to the flagellum
Along the flagellum, the middle piece, principal piece and end piece have decreasing diameters
questions.explanation: The energy supply (mitochondrial sheath) is in the middle piece, not the end piece; the flagellum narrows from middle piece to principal piece to end piece.

questions.stem: Under the light microscope, the spermatozoon shows three parts:
options: Head, neck, flagellum
Head, acrosome, tail
Head, middle piece, end piece
Nucleus, acrosome, flagellum
questions.explanation: The three visible parts are the head, the neck (the narrow portion joining head and flagellum) and the flagellum; the acrosome belongs to the head and the middle/end pieces belong to the flagellum.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man has both testes still in the abdomen (bilateral cryptorchidism). Which finding(s) is (are) expected?
options: Seminiferous tubules almost devoid of gametes
Maintained testosterone production by the Leydig cells
Loss of male secondary sexual characteristics
Sterility
questions.explanation: Undescended testes produce no spermatozoa (sterility) but their interstitial Leydig cells keep secreting testosterone, so secondary sexual characteristics are preserved.

questions.stem: Why does an undescended (cryptorchid) testis fail to produce spermatozoa?
options: Normal spermatogenesis needs the slight cooling obtained when the testes migrate into the scrotum
Its Leydig cells stop secreting testosterone
It contains no Sertoli cells
The pituitary stops secreting FSH
questions.explanation: The lesson attributes the arrest to the lack of scrotal cooling; testosterone secretion by Leydig cells is maintained.

questions.stem: About the neuroendocrine control of the testis:
options: GnRH is produced in a pulsatile way by hypothalamic neurons, and its production greatly increases at puberty
GnRH acts directly on Sertoli cells
LH ensures the multiplication of Leydig cells
Free testosterone exerts negative feedback on LH secretion
questions.explanation: GnRH acts on the pituitary, triggering FSH and LH secretion; it does not act on the testis directly. LH drives Leydig cells, and free testosterone feeds back negatively on LH (via the hypothalamus or the pituitary).

questions.stem: About inhibin:
options: It is secreted by Sertoli cells in response to FSH
It is secreted by Leydig cells
It exerts negative feedback on LH secretion
It can act directly on the pituitary gonadotroph cells, or indirectly by decreasing GnRH secretion
questions.explanation: FSH triggers inhibin secretion by Sertoli cells, and inhibin lowers FSH secretion (hypothalamus or pituitary). The negative feedback on LH comes from free testosterone.

questions.stem: A semen analysis concludes oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (OATS). This means:
options: Oligozoospermia: the spermatozoa are too few to fertilize an oocyte
Asthenozoospermia: the spermatozoa have an abnormal shape
Teratozoospermia: the spermatozoa have an abnormal shape
A varicocele is among its possible causes
questions.explanation: Astheno- refers to weak motility, terato- to abnormal shape. Causes listed include genital infections, varicocele, smoking, obesity, heat, radiation, medications and stress.

questions.stem: About the factors influencing spermatogenesis:
options: About 25% of men who contract mumps after puberty become infertile
Endocrine disorders account for most cases of male infertility
Some men produce antibodies against their own spermatozoa, causing poor motility or agglutination
Anticancer treatments affect spermatogenesis only temporarily
questions.explanation: Endocrine disorders explain only about 2–5% of male infertility, and radiation or anticancer treatments may act temporarily or permanently.

questions.stem: From the standpoint of chromosomal complement, about spermatozoa:
options: Meiosis yields equal numbers of 22 + X and 22 + Y spermatozoa
X- and Y-bearing spermatozoa can be distinguished morphologically
X- and Y-bearing spermatozoa can be separated in vitro
Their highly compacted haploid genome protects them against genotoxic agents
questions.explanation: Separating the XY pair at meiosis gives equal numbers of X- and Y-bearing spermatozoa, which look identical but can be separated in vitro.
